questions.q: What is the core difference between value-based and policy-based reinforcement learning?
options: Value-based methods learn Q(s,a) and derive a policy from it; policy-based methods learn the policy pi_theta(a|s) directly
Policy-based methods never use neural networks
Value-based methods only work in continuous action spaces
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: Value-based methods (like DQN) act by taking the argmax of a learned Q-function. Policy-based methods parameterize and optimize the policy itself directly.

questions.q: Why do policy gradient methods map more naturally onto large language models than value-based methods do?
options: LLMs cannot be trained with gradients
An LLM already outputs a probability distribution over the next token, making it inherently a stochastic policy
Value-based methods require continuous action spaces
LLMs have no notion of state
questions.explain: Since an LLM produces a probability distribution over next tokens given context, it is already structured like a stochastic policy pi_theta(a|s), which is exactly what policy gradient methods optimize directly.

questions.q: According to the policy gradient theorem, what does the gradient of expected return look like?
options: E[grad_theta log pi_theta(a|s) * Q_pi(s,a)]
The gradient of the reward function with respect to the environment's transition probabilities
max_a Q(s,a) minus the average reward
The second derivative of the value function
questions.explain: The policy gradient theorem expresses the gradient of expected return as the expectation of the gradient of the log-probability of actions, weighted by how good those actions were (Q^pi(s,a)).

questions.q: In the policy gradient update, what happens to the probability of an action that led to a high return?
options: It is pushed down, to encourage exploration
It is pushed up, since the gradient step increases log-probability weighted by positive return
It is left completely unchanged
It is set to exactly 1.0
questions.explain: The score-function gradient weights the log-probability gradient by the action's return, so actions that led to high return get their probability increased.

questions.q: In a PyTorch policy network for discrete actions, what role does Categorical(logits=logits) play?
options: It computes the Q-value for each action
It wraps the network's raw outputs into a probability distribution that can be sampled from and scored with log_prob
It directly outputs the single best action deterministically
It replaces the need for a replay buffer in all RL algorithms
questions.explain: Categorical(logits=logits) turns raw network outputs into a proper probability distribution over actions, enabling stochastic sampling via .sample() and the log pi_theta(a|s) term via .log_prob().
